identification: The Atlas of Living Australia and the Australian Faunal Directory use Jacky Lizard for Amphibolurus muricatus (White, 1790). iNaturalist uses Jacky Dragon. The Directory lists the species for Victoria, including the Victorian Volcanic Plain and the Victorian Midlands, and its ecological descriptors include arboreal, diurnal, low open woodland, open forest, open scrub, oviparous, tall open forest, terrestrial and woodland (https://biodiversity.org.au/afd/taxa/Amphibolurus_muricatus). Museums Victoria describes a grey to dark brown body with darker triangular patches that often form a zigzag, an orange-yellow mouth interior, a small crest along the back of the neck, and a snout-to-base-of-tail length up to 12 cm (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8368). A direct HTML fetch of that Museums Victoria page returned HTTP 403. The description is the indexed text of the same URL. One Earth Guardians row inside 5 km carries the observer's own words, 'im fairly certain these are jacky lizards due to a previous identification' (https://biocache-ws.ala.org.au/ws/occurrence/1517ac85-d50b-4ed6-b11a-3481501f1c50). That row stays in the count. It is not a museum identification.
habitat: Museums Victoria says these lizards live in sclerophyll forests and coastal woodlands, usually where there is some native vegetation, bask on logs, fallen branches or rocks, and run into leaf litter or under trees or logs when startled (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8368). The Directory's habitat words are low open woodland, open forest, open scrub, tall open forest and woodland (https://biodiversity.org.au/afd/taxa/Amphibolurus_muricatus). Named local remarks match that cover. On 19 October 2014 at Inverleigh Conservation Reserve a lizard was lying over the hole of its burrow on the edge of Old Teesdale Track (https://biocache-ws.ala.org.au/ws/occurrence/7e3633bb-ff7c-4c62-b461-b3dd60ed89c1). On 25 September 2019 at Inverleigh NCR one was initially among short grass in a little sunshine and scurried into a thicket of Lepidosperma and fallen branches (https://biocache-ws.ala.org.au/ws/occurrence/bafedea6-aa7f-457a-ad79-71d16e953058). The Friends of Inverleigh Nature Conservation Reserve describe the reserve, not a lizard study: about 1,050 ha between Inverleigh and Teesdale, dominant trees Manna Gum (Eucalyptus viminalis) and River Red Gum (Eucalyptus camaldulensis), a ground layer dominated by wallaby grass, and grassy woodland classed as an endangered ecological vegetation class (https://inverleigh.org.au/features/nature-conservation/). In the 5–10 km ring a 10 November 2018 note at Bannockburn Bush Reserve says the animal had been basking on fallen logs and dashed to cover (https://biocache-ws.ala.org.au/ws/occurrence/e309e009-8ea0-4889-8ad7-3161dce82fb0). An OzAtlas row at the Bannockburn tile coordinate says two small individuals were found during a tile grid survey (https://biocache-ws.ala.org.au/ws/occurrence/209bd688-d682-4384-bcd2-84219c731f0a). Tiles are a survey shelter, not natural habitat.
diet: Museums Victoria says the diet is a wide range of small arthropods and lists it as carnivore, insects and invertebrates (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8368). No Inverleigh, Teesdale or Bannockburn record opened here names a prey animal. Snail-bait warnings written for blue-tongues are not a diet statement for this dragon.
activeSeason: Museums Victoria says Jacky Dragons are active during the day and are often seen basking (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8368). The Directory also marks the species diurnal (https://biodiversity.org.au/afd/taxa/Amphibolurus_muricatus). The circle is not an activity study. Inside 5 km the eight ALA rows fall in October (3), September (2), November (2) and December (1), from 1998 to 2023. Inside 10 km the month facet adds April (2) and one each in March and August, across 1998–2024 and 19 rows. An obscured iNaturalist note, which cannot be mapped, says 'Cool day, curled up' on 12 April 2022 (https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/113365587). That is one anecdote, not a season.
breeding: The Australian Faunal Directory marks Amphibolurus muricatus oviparous, which means egg-laying (https://biodiversity.org.au/afd/taxa/Amphibolurus_muricatus). Clutch size, mating month and nest site are not on that page or on the Museums Victoria extract. They are left blank rather than taken from a general book. No local record is described as a nest or a clutch.

threats: No Jacky Lizard row opened in this circle describes a cat, a dog, a mower, snail bait or a road death. Museums Victoria's disturbance note is that a startled animal runs into leaf litter or under trees or logs (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8368). The local notes say the same kind of thing: into Lepidosperma and fallen branches, or off logs into cover. Cat, dog, mower, snail-pellet and road harm is documented for blue-tongues on the eastern-blue-tongue, blotched-blue-tongue and lizard-friendly-garden objects. It is not repeated here as a Jacky injury series. All native reptiles are protected. The Conservation Regulator says it is illegal under the Wildlife Act 1975 to wilfully disturb, hunt, take, trap or kill wildlife without a permit (https://www.vic.gov.au/authority-control-wildlife-application-guide). Routine mowing or driving that unintentionally disturbs wildlife does not by itself require an Authority to Control Wildlife. Relocating wildlife does.
conservation: A text search of the Flora and Fauna Guarantee Act Threatened List, July 2026, found no Amphibolurus muricatus and no Jacky Lizard (https://www.environment.vic.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0028/793801/FFG_Threatened_List_July_2026.pdf). The EPBC threatened-species extract dated 28 August 2026 has no row for Amphibolurus muricatus (https://data.gov.au/data/dataset/ae652011-f39e-4c6c-91b8-1dc2d2dfee8f/resource/78401dce-1f40-49d3-92c4-3713d6e34974/download/20260828spcs.csv). Absence from those lists does not remove Wildlife Act protection (https://www.vic.gov.au/authority-control-wildlife-application-guide). The IUCN Red List page was not opened, so no IUCN category is stated.

identification: The Australian Faunal Directory name is Eastern Three-lined Skink, Acritoscincus duperreyi (Gray, 1838). The Directory lists Victoria, including the Victorian Volcanic Plain and the Victorian Midlands. The original combination on that page is Tiliqua duperreyi (https://biodiversity.org.au/afd/taxa/Acritoscincus_duperreyi). Museums Victoria describes a grey or metallic brown body, a wide black stripe along the side, a throat that is often orange-red, a snout-vent length up to 6 cm, and a maximum size field of 10 cm (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/15610). A direct HTML fetch of that page returned HTTP 403. The description is the indexed text of the same URL. An iNaturalist description, 'flashes of gold colour in the sun', is an observer's note on observation 63947284. It is not a field mark from the museum page (https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/63947284).
habitat: Museums Victoria says the habitat is woodlands, grasslands and heathlands, and that the skink may climb low grass tussocks or shrubs to bask (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/15610). The Directory page that was fetched lists the bioregions and does not add a separate habitat sentence (https://biodiversity.org.au/afd/taxa/Acritoscincus_duperreyi). The one named shelter inside 5 km is a Geelong Field Naturalists Club note on 10 March 2018 at Inverleigh Nature Conservation Reserve: two animals, 'Found under logs and metal debris' (https://biocache-ws.ala.org.au/ws/occurrence/0488ca06-fb4f-4d50-a064-f4dcf46af421). Metal debris is what the note says. It is not a claim that debris is the natural habitat. The reserve's trees and wallaby-grass ground layer are described by the Friends of the reserve (https://inverleigh.org.au/features/nature-conservation/). In the outer ring, Victorian Biodiversity Atlas localities are paddocks off Harvey Road at Bannockburn, and one 1989 locality 'ROUGHLY 6 KM SW OF LOWNDE BRIDGE'. An OzAtlas row on 12 September 2018 says 'Found during a tile grid survey' at the Bannockburn tile coordinate (https://biocache-ws.ala.org.au/ws/occurrence/77e2578a-d49e-4134-b5c3-6801a2f17514). A tile is a survey shelter.
diet: Museums Victoria lists the diet as invertebrates and insects (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/15610). No local record names a prey animal.
activeSeason: The Museums Victoria habitat line says these skinks may climb low grass tussocks or shrubs to bask, which is daytime behaviour, but that page extract does not use the word diurnal and the Directory page that was fetched does not list an activity descriptor (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/15610; https://biodiversity.org.au/afd/taxa/Acritoscincus_duperreyi). Record dates are not a survey. Inside 5 km the four rows are March (2) and October (2), 2018–2022. Inside 10 km the 11 rows run 1989–2025 and include June and July as well as January, March, September, October and November. Winter-dated rows exist, so this file does not say the species is only seen in summer.
breeding: Museums Victoria says up to three females may nest together, each laying a clutch of up to five eggs (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/15610). That is egg-laying. No local record describes a nest. Clutch figures other than 'up to five', and any statement about temperature-dependent sex determination, were not taken from a page opened for this file.

identification: Lampropholis guichenoti (Duméril & Bibron, 1839) is the Pale-flecked Garden Sunskink on the Australian Faunal Directory and on ALA. The Directory lists Victoria, including the Victorian Volcanic Plain and the Victorian Midlands, and the ecological descriptors diurnal, low open woodland, open forest, oviparous, tall forest, terrestrial and woodland (https://biodiversity.org.au/afd/taxa/Lampropholis_guichenoti). Museums Victoria describes a small grey-brown or olive-brown skink, usually with a dark brown stripe down the back from the neck to the tail and a dark brown stripe from the side of the neck to the tail, often speckled, belly whitish or silvery-grey, snout-vent length up to 6 cm, maximum size field 10 cm. Another name on that page is Common Grass Skink (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/12372). A direct HTML fetch returned HTTP 403. The description is the indexed text of the same URL. The dropped-tail photograph in this circle is iNaturalist 61371538, identified only to the family Scincidae, not to this species (https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/61371538). Tail-dropping is not attributed to the garden skink from that photo.
habitat: Museums Victoria says the species is found from wet and dry sclerophyll forest to coastal and mountain heaths, and is commonly found in suburban gardens. The page spells sclerophyll as 'schlerophyll'. The same page says the animals are often found basking or foraging among leaf litter and rock piles (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/12372). The Directory's habitat words are low open woodland, open forest, tall forest and woodland (https://biodiversity.org.au/afd/taxa/Lampropholis_guichenoti). Inside 5 km the only reserve name is iNaturalist 71591617, place guess Inverleigh Nature Conservation Reserve, accuracy about 2,515 m, so the reserve is named and the point is not a precise log (https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/71591617). The same coarse coordinate is shared with the blotched blue-tongue observation 267125999. The 1989 VBA locality is 'ROUGHLY 4 KM S OF TEESDALE', not a named garden. In the outer ring most precise public points are at Bannockburn, including place guess Bannockburn Bush on observation 61357688. OzAtlas rows at -38.052582, 144.134824 are the Bannockburn tile-grid coordinate. One of them, 12 September 2018, says 'Found during a tile grid survey' (https://biocache-ws.ala.org.au/ws/occurrence/7955ddc0-7052-4274-a5e2-8c5def0dd96d). The 16 October 2017 row (17 animals) and the 12 November 2017 row (6 animals) share that coordinate and have no remark of their own. They are not added to the 7 animals on the 2018 row, and they are not a town population.
diet: Museums Victoria says garden skinks feed on small invertebrates (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/12372). No local record names a prey animal. An iNaturalist note that an animal was about 8 cm long on the edge of a track is a size and position note, not a diet (https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/39606193).
activeSeason: Museums Victoria and the Directory both say the species is diurnal (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/12372; https://biodiversity.org.au/afd/taxa/Lampropholis_guichenoti). Record months are not a survey. Inside 5 km the four rows are March (2), April (1) and July (1), 1989–2023. Inside 10 km the 17 rows include July as well, and also January, February, March, April, September, October, November and December, 1989–2025. A July record means this file does not say the species is absent in winter.
breeding: The Directory marks the species oviparous (https://biodiversity.org.au/afd/taxa/Lampropholis_guichenoti). Museums Victoria says females congregate to lay eggs in communal nests, which can contain more than 200 eggs, with up to four eggs per female (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/12372). No nest was described in the Inverleigh or Bannockburn rows opened here. The communal-nest figure is the museum account, not a local count.

The public coordinate falls about 3.87 km from the centre and is not a hangout. OzAtlas, 29 March 2018, one animal, Trevor Pescott, no locality, -38.062941, 144.056702, about 4.16 km (https://biocache-ws.ala.org.au/ws/occurrence/e61aa129-5076-4f46-a9da-b6b4095c43b6). identification: Both blue-tongue species in the Inverleigh circle are skinks, not snakes. Wildlife Victoria says Victoria has the eastern or common blue-tongue, Tiliqua scincoides, and the blotched blue-tongue, Tiliqua nigrolutea, both common in residential areas, and that the long body, small legs and large head can make them look like snakes. Eastern animals are stripy. Blotched animals are blotchy. Both have a blue tongue used as a warning (https://wildlifevictoria.org.au/learn/native-species-post/blue-tongued-lizard/). The Australian Museum separates them by pattern. The eastern blue-tongue is silvery-grey with broad dark brown or blackish bands across the back and tail. Animals on the coast usually have a black stripe between the eye and the ear, which may continue along the side of the neck. It can grow to almost 600 mm in total length, of which about 360 mm is head and body (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/reptiles/eastern-blue-tongue-lizard/). The blotched blue-tongue, on that same eastern page, is dark chocolate brown to black with large pink, cream or yellow blotches on the back, and a tail banded in the same colours. The blotched page itself describes a long body, large head, short legs and toes, and a tail shorter than the body (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/reptiles/blotched-blue-tongue-lizard/). DEECA rehabilitation guidelines use the same split: eastern animals grey with brown stripes and a black line behind the eye; blotched animals brown to black with uneven blotches and a lack of a black line behind the eye (https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0026/671264/Part-B-Reptiles-Amphibians-Chapter1.pdf; https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0023/668120/Victorian-Wildlife-Rehabilitation-Guidelines-Part-B-Reptiles-and-Amphibians.pdf). Those guideline sentences are from the indexed text of the PDFs. Museums Victoria's eastern page says snout to base of tail up to 35 cm, maximum size field 45 cm, other name Common Blue-tongue, and hazard 'Usually harmless, but can bite' (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8399). HTML fetch of that page returned HTTP 403. The Australian Museum's distribution paragraph for the eastern species, as fetched, describes New South Wales and the Sydney region. That paragraph is not used as the species' range. The Directory lists Tiliqua scincoides for Victoria, and the local records are Victorian (https://biodiversity.org.au/afd/taxa/Tiliqua_scincoides). The northern subspecies Tiliqua scincoides intermedia is a different animal on the EPBC list and is not marked for Victoria. It is not the animal in these rows.
habitat: The Australian Museum says blue-tongues usually live in open country with tussocky grasses or leaf litter, shelter at night among leaf litter or under rocks and logs, bask in the morning and then forage, and keep an active body temperature of about 30–35°C. In cold weather they remain inactive, buried in shelter, but may bask on sunny days (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/reptiles/eastern-blue-tongue-lizard/). The same shelter text is on the blotched page. Wildlife Victoria says they live in mountain forests, coastal heathlands and suburban gardens, are active during the day, and prefer low shrubby or tall grassy areas with places to hide, and bask on concrete, stone or brick (https://wildlifevictoria.org.au/learn/native-species-post/blue-tongued-lizard/). Museums Victoria's eastern habitat line is dry sclerophyll forest, open montane woodland and grassland, and coastal heathlands (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8399). The Directory's descriptors include diurnal, low open shrubland, low open woodland, low woodland, omnivore, open forest, open heath, open scrub, terrestrial, viviparous and woodland, and the states include Victoria (https://biodiversity.org.au/afd/taxa/Tiliqua_scincoides). DEECA's Common Blue-tongued Lizard sheet, indexed from the PDF because a direct download returned HTTP 403, says they shelter at night under logs or leaf litter and debris and warm themselves in sunny areas, and are mostly inactive in the colder months (https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0019/84106/Common-Blue-tongued-Lizard.pdf). The only named reserve-side locality inside the wider circle is Inverleigh Common, and one roadkill note names farmland with drooping sheoak roadside vegetation on Spring Creek Road. Those are record notes, not a habitat study. The Inverleigh Nature Conservation Reserve's manna gum, river red gum and wallaby grass are the reserve description where other lizards were recorded (https://inverleigh.org.au/features/nature-conservation/). No eastern blue-tongue row inside 5 km uses the reserve's name.
diet: The Australian Museum says blue-tongues eat a wide variety of plants and animals, mostly slow-moving, and that large teeth and strong jaws crush snail shells and beetles (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/reptiles/eastern-blue-tongue-lizard/). Museums Victoria lists insects, snails, carrion, wildflowers, native fruits and berries, and the same crushing jaws (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8399). Wildlife Victoria lists insects, snails, berries and native wildflowers (https://wildlifevictoria.org.au/learn/native-species-post/blue-tongued-lizard/). The DEECA sheet adds beetles and says they reduce snails and slugs, and says never to feed them (https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0019/84106/Common-Blue-tongued-Lizard.pdf). Rehabilitation diet tables that include mealworms, mice and a vegetable mix are captive feeding, not a wild diet (https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0026/671264/Part-B-Reptiles-Amphibians-Chapter1.pdf). No local record names a meal.
activeSeason: The Australian Museum, Wildlife Victoria, Museums Victoria, the Directory and the DEECA sheet all describe daytime activity, with morning basking and foraging later, and inactivity in cold weather with possible sunny-day basking (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/reptiles/eastern-blue-tongue-lizard/; https://wildlifevictoria.org.au/learn/native-species-post/blue-tongued-lizard/). The circle is not a season study. Inside 5 km the rows are January and December only, 1998 and 2015. Inside 10 km the 11 rows, 1996–2020, fall in January, May, September, October, November and December. A May roadkill note says the animal was presumably attracted out by warm sunny days (https://biocache-ws.ala.org.au/ws/occurrence/9b700ea7-d2dd-42c7-bee6-9db904035adb).
breeding: The Directory marks Tiliqua scincoides viviparous, live-bearing (https://biodiversity.org.au/afd/taxa/Tiliqua_scincoides). The Australian Museum says female blue-tongues give birth three to five months after mating, between December and April, and that the eastern blue-tongue usually gives birth between December and January. Embryos develop with a placenta. Young eat the membranes, shed within a few days, and disperse within a few days. Of all the blue-tongues, the eastern species has the largest litters and the smallest young: up to 19, but usually about 10, each 130–140 mm total length and 10–20 g. The museum says eastern blue-tongues probably become adults at about three years and about 400 mm total length, and that several captives have lived 20 years and may live much longer. Males pursue females from September to November (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/reptiles/eastern-blue-tongue-lizard/). Museums Victoria says live-bearing, up to 19 young (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8399). Wildlife Victoria says breeding from September to November and up to 25 live young between December and January, young self-sufficient and leaving after a few days, and males able to father several litters a season, and separately says they can live up to 30 years in the wild (https://wildlifevictoria.org.au/learn/native-species-post/blue-tongued-lizard/). The DEECA sheet says young are born self-sufficient, disperse within a few days, and are sexually mature at four years (https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0019/84106/Common-Blue-tongued-Lizard.pdf). The indexed rehabilitation profile for the blotched blue-tongue, not a separate eastern litter, gives male maturity over 1 year, female maturity over 2 years, and longevity 12–15 years (https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0023/668120/Victorian-Wildlife-Rehabilitation-Guidelines-Part-B-Reptiles-and-Amphibians.pdf). A 2017 Land for Wildlife note, after describing a Tasmanian mating study, says blue-tongues give birth to two or three live young (https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/protecting-wildlife/land-for-wildlife/LFW_Newsletter_2017_01.pdf). These litter, maturity and lifespan figures are not averaged. No local record is a birth.

threats: The Australian Museum says blue-tongues eat snails and slugs poisoned by snail baits and can be poisoned themselves, and that a neighbour's chemicals matter because animals squeeze through fences. When long grass is mowed they hide in the grass rather than running. They bask on warm black roads (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/reptiles/eastern-blue-tongue-lizard/). Wildlife Victoria says snail bait is extremely dangerous and to call (03) 8400 7300 if a lizard has consumed it. The same page says dog and cat attacks are among the common reports and can kill by wounds, blood loss, or infection from saliva in puncture wounds (https://wildlifevictoria.org.au/learn/native-species-post/blue-tongued-lizard/). The museum also lists feral cats and dogs, and says young animals are easy prey for suburban dogs and cats, and that a few adults are killed by large dogs (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/reptiles/eastern-blue-tongue-lizard/). The DEECA sheet says leave logs and rocks, reduce or eliminate snail bait because poisoned snails and slugs poison the lizard, drive carefully because they lie on roads and are slow, keep cats indoors at night, never dump cats, and never feed them (https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0019/84106/Common-Blue-tongued-Lizard.pdf). Better Health Channel says do not place baits where children, pets or native animals can reach them (https://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/pest-control-in-the-home). The only local injury note is the 25 May 2017 roadkill on Spring Creek Road. No local snail-bait death, cat attack or mower injury was found in the rows. A frightened blue-tongue may bite if picked up. The Australian Museum says the bite can hurt, break the skin and bruise, and that there is no venom; clean the site as for any animal bite (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/reptiles/eastern-blue-tongue-lizard/). Museums Victoria says usually harmless, but can bite (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8399). Wildlife Victoria says they do not bite and pose no danger to humans or pets (https://wildlifevictoria.org.au/learn/native-species-post/blue-tongued-lizard/). Those sentences disagree. The cautious public line is the museum one: not venomous, and may bite if picked up. If a pet attacks a lizard, Wildlife Victoria's number is (03) 8400 7300. Zoos Victoria's emergency page lists the same Wildlife Victoria number and DEECA on 136 186 (https://www.zoo.org.au/emergency-wildlife-help/). Native reptiles are protected, and relocating wildlife needs an authorisation even though Wildlife Victoria describes moving a blue-tongue a short distance from a dog with a towel (https://www.vic.gov.au/authority-control-wildlife-application-guide; https://wildlifevictoria.org.au/learn/native-species-post/blue-tongued-lizard/).
conservation: A text search of the FFG Threatened List, July 2026, found no Tiliqua scincoides (https://www.environment.vic.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0028/793801/FFG_Threatened_List_July_2026.pdf). The EPBC extract of 28 August 2026 has no row for Tiliqua scincoides. It does list Tiliqua scincoides intermedia, the Northern Blue-tongued Skink, as Critically Endangered. On that row the Victoria column is blank, and the Northern Territory, Queensland and Western Australia columns are marked. That subspecies is not these Inverleigh records (https://data.gov.au/data/dataset/ae652011-f39e-4c6c-91b8-1dc2d2dfee8f/resource/78401dce-1f40-49d3-92c4-3713d6e34974/download/20260828spcs.csv). The rehabilitation guideline word 'Common' is a profile label, not an FFG category. Wildlife Act protection still applies (https://www.vic.gov.au/authority-control-wildlife-application-guide). The IUCN page was not opened. No Zoos Victoria species page for this lizard was found. The zoo page used here is the emergency-help page only.
notWellDocumented: Litter size is up to 19, usually about 10, on the Australian Museum eastern page and Museums Victoria. Wildlife Victoria says up to 25. A Land for Wildlife note says two or three. They are not averaged.

Age at maturity is about three years on the Australian Museum eastern page, four years on the DEECA sheet, and over 1 year for males and over 2 years for females on the indexed blotched rehabilitation profile.
Lifespan is captive 20 years and perhaps longer on the museum page, up to 30 years in the wild on Wildlife Victoria, and 12–15 years on the indexed blotched rehabilitation profile.
Wildlife Victoria says blue-tongues do not bite. The Australian Museum and Museums Victoria say they can bite if handled or picked up. There is no venom in the museum account.
The Australian Museum eastern distribution paragraph that was fetched is written for New South Wales. Victorian occurrence rests on the Directory, Wildlife Victoria and the local records.
DEECA species-sheet and rehabilitation-guideline sentences are indexed PDF text. Direct download of the species sheet returned HTTP 403.
The January 2015 pair is one sighting with 977 m accuracy. The town name Inverleigh is not a street.
The November 2018 VBA point with 10 m uncertainty is the copy of an obscured iNaturalist observation and is not a public site.
The 1996 Teesdale row has no individual count.

records.note: ALA vernacular is Southern Blue-tongue. The Australian Faunal Directory lists Blotched Blue-tongue and Southern Blue-tongue. iNaturalist, Museums Victoria and Wildlife Victoria use Blotched Blue-tongue or Blotched Bluetongue. The supplied counts match: 1 inside 5 km and 2 inside 10 km, both iNaturalist Australia. There is no VBA row. Do not add ALA and iNaturalist totals. identification: Use the same split as for the eastern blue-tongue. The Australian Museum says the blotched blue-tongue is dark chocolate brown to black with large pink, cream or yellow blotches on the back, and a tail banded in those colours, while the eastern animal has broad dark bands and usually a black stripe between the eye and the ear (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/reptiles/eastern-blue-tongue-lizard/; https://australian.museum/learn/animals/reptiles/blotched-blue-tongue-lizard/). Wildlife Victoria says eastern animals are stripy and blotched animals are blotchy (https://wildlifevictoria.org.au/learn/native-species-post/blue-tongued-lizard/). DEECA rehabilitation text says blotched animals lack the black line behind the eye (https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0023/668120/Victorian-Wildlife-Rehabilitation-Guidelines-Part-B-Reptiles-and-Amphibians.pdf). Museums Victoria describes a cream, yellow or pinkish underside with black mottling, limbs speckled black and white, and snout to base of tail up to 37 cm (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8397). HTML fetch of that page returned HTTP 403. The description is the indexed text. The Australian Museum says some individuals may weigh more than 1 kg, and gives a size range of 550 mm on that page (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/reptiles/blotched-blue-tongue-lizard/). The Directory lists both common names and includes Victoria and the Victorian Volcanic Plain (https://biodiversity.org.au/afd/taxa/Tiliqua_nigrolutea). The museum's blotched range sentence runs from Tasmania through Victoria to the Blue Mountains of New South Wales, widespread in southern lowlands and more montane further north (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/reptiles/blotched-blue-tongue-lizard/).
habitat: The shared Australian Museum account is open country with tussocky grasses or leaf litter, night shelter under leaf litter, rocks and logs, and morning basking (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/reptiles/blotched-blue-tongue-lizard/). Museums Victoria's blotched habitat line is wet and dry sclerophyll forest, montane woodlands and coastal heathlands (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8397). The Directory's descriptors include alpine, diurnal, omnivore, open forest, tall forest, terrestrial, viviparous and woodland (https://biodiversity.org.au/afd/taxa/Tiliqua_nigrolutea). Rehabilitation profiles add suburban gardens, built-up areas, forest and grassland, and a home range of 0.5–2 ha for the blotched profile (https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0023/668120/Victorian-Wildlife-Rehabilitation-Guidelines-Part-B-Reptiles-and-Amphibians.pdf). That home-range figure is the guideline, not a measurement at Inverleigh. The 2021 observation names Inverleigh Nature Conservation Reserve only as a place guess with about 2.5 km accuracy. The reserve's manna gum, river red gum and wallaby grass are the Friends' description of the reserve, not a lizard study (https://inverleigh.org.au/features/nature-conservation/). The 2024 observation's place guess is Teesdale VIC 3328. It does not name a street.
diet: The Australian Museum's shared text is plants and animals, mostly slow-moving, with jaws that crush snail shells and beetles (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/reptiles/blotched-blue-tongue-lizard/). The Museums Victoria blotched biology extract, from the collections search snippet of the same species, includes insects, snails, carrion, wildflowers, native fruits and berries. The species-page index also lists diet as omnivore, insects, invertebrates and fruit (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8397). Rehabilitation text lists snails, slugs, grasshoppers, beetles, fruit, fungi, berries and flowers (https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0023/668120/Victorian-Wildlife-Rehabilitation-Guidelines-Part-B-Reptiles-and-Amphibians.pdf). No local record names a meal. Snail bait is a poisoning route because they eat snails and slugs, not because a local death was found.
activeSeason: The Australian Museum, the Directory and the rehabilitation profile say blue-tongues are diurnal, inactive in cold weather, and may bask on sunny days (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/reptiles/blotched-blue-tongue-lizard/; https://biodiversity.org.au/afd/taxa/Tiliqua_nigrolutea). The only local months are October 2021 and September 2024. Two rows are not a season.
breeding: The Directory marks the species viviparous (https://biodiversity.org.au/afd/taxa/Tiliqua_nigrolutea). The Australian Museum blotched page says females give birth three to five months after mating, between December and April, with a placenta, and that young disperse within a few days. It does not repeat the eastern page's 'up to 19, usually about 10' (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/reptiles/blotched-blue-tongue-lizard/). Museums Victoria's blotched page says live-bearing, up to 25 young (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8397). Wildlife Victoria's general blue-tongue page also says up to 25 between December and January (https://wildlifevictoria.org.au/learn/native-species-post/blue-tongued-lizard/). The eastern museum litter is not copied onto this species. Rehabilitation text for the blotched profile says mating in spring, gestation 3–5 months, live-bearing, male maturity over 1 year, female over 2 years, longevity 12–15 years, weight 300–500 g and length 35–50 cm (https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0023/668120/Victorian-Wildlife-Rehabilitation-Guidelines-Part-B-Reptiles-and-Amphibians.pdf). The museum's general blue-tongue line about adulthood at about three years and captive life of 20 years is also on the blotched page and is not reconciled with the guideline. identification: The Australian Faunal Directory name is White's Skink, Liopholis whitii (Lacépède, 1804). The Directory lists Victoria, including the Victorian Volcanic Plain and the Victorian Midlands, and the descriptors diurnal, low open woodland, open forest, saxicoline, tall forest, viviparous and woodland. Saxicoline means rock-dwelling (https://biodiversity.org.au/afd/taxa/Liopholis_whitii). Museums Victoria describes a grey-brown skink with a red-brown flush toward the tail. Some animals are unpatterned above. Others have two broad black stripes along the back with white or yellow spots between them. The sides are plain or mottled with black-edged pale spots. The underside is white to light grey. A pale streak runs from above the mouth to the ear, passing under the eye. Snout to base of tail is up to 11 cm, and the maximum-size field on that page is also 11 cm (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/10627). A direct HTML fetch returned HTTP 403. The description is the indexed text of the same URL. The 1995 record does not describe pattern, so the animal was not matched to the striped or the plain form from a photo in this file.
habitat: Museums Victoria says White's Skinks prefer rocky habitats with a well-developed canopy, bask or forage on rocky outcrops, and shelter in burrows under rock slabs or logs. The habitat line is rocky microhabitats near rock outcrops in open woodland, dry forests and coastal heathlands (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/10627). The Directory's saxicoline descriptor agrees that rocks are part of the species account (https://biodiversity.org.au/afd/taxa/Liopholis_whitii). The only local row says '7 km S of Inverleigh'. It does not say the animals were on a rock, under a slab, or in a burrow. The rock habitat is the museum account, not this record.
diet: Museums Victoria says they feed on invertebrates (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/10627). The 1995 record does not name prey.
activeSeason: Museums Victoria and the Directory say the species is active during the day (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/10627; https://biodiversity.org.au/afd/taxa/Liopholis_whitii). The only local date is 22 August 1995. One August row is not a statement that the species is a winter specialist, and it is not a full activity calendar.
breeding: The Directory marks the species viviparous (https://biodiversity.org.au/afd/taxa/Liopholis_whitii). Museums Victoria says females give birth to live young rather than laying eggs, with one to three offspring each brood (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/10627). The local row is two animals captured and released. It is not described as a mother and young, so it is not read as a brood.
hangouts: There is no record inside 5 km. The one record inside 10 km is Victorian Biodiversity Atlas, 22 August 1995, individual count 2, captured and released, Philip Du Guesclin, locality '7 km S of Inverleigh', coordinate -38.15545, 144.05392, about 6.18 km from -38.10, 144.05, uncertainty 100 m, occurrence 175117653 (https://biocache-ws.ala.org.au/ws/occurrence/613ed93b-854b-43fa-b7a0-eb5da8ae589b). A different VBA row, 24 January 2007, 'fam. Scincidae gen. Egernia', one animal, Cath Grant, 'Paddock off Harvey Rd, Bannockburn', about 8.65 km, is unidentified to species and is not White's Skink (https://biocache-ws.ala.org.au/ws/occurrence/966a4fe1-cf9d-4a11-b7da-ce4351ed7e6a).
threats: No threat is written on the 1995 record. Museums Victoria says that if disturbed they retreat quickly (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/10627). Cat, dog, mower, snail-bait and road harm documented for blue-tongues is not copied here as a White's Skink injury. identification: The Australian Faunal Directory lists Many-lined Delma and Striped Legless Lizard for Delma impar. States include Victoria. Bioregions include the Victorian Volcanic Plain, the Victorian Midlands, the South East Coastal Plain and the South Eastern Highlands. Ecological descriptors on the page fetched are low open woodland, noctidiurnal, open forest and oviparous (https://biodiversity.org.au/afd/taxa/Delma_impar). iNaturalist's common name for taxon 36937 is Many-lined Delma. Museums Victoria's preferred name is Striped Legless Lizard, with other name Many-lined Delma. That page describes one or several dark stripes along each side, a tongue that is not forked, visible ears, and snout-vent length up to 9 cm. It places the animal in infraorder Gekkota, family Pygopodidae (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8389). HTML fetch returned HTTP 403. The description is the indexed text. SPRAT's indexed profile says a pale-grey lizard up to 30 cm in length, maximum snout-vent length about 12 cm, external ear openings, a fleshy undivided tongue, and a tail longer than the body, and that the hind limbs are small flaps beside the vent (https://www.environment.gov.au/cgi-bin/sprat/public/publicspecies.pl?taxon_id=1649). The 9 cm and about 12 cm snout-vent figures are not reconciled. The conservation advice describes a pale grey-brown back, a cream underside, and dark brown or blackish stripes, and says it is distinguished from other Delma by 13–16 mid-body scale rows and fusion or partial fusion of the nasal and first supralabial scales (https://www.environment.gov.au/biodiversity/threatened/species/pubs/1649-conservation-advice-16122016.pdf). Direct SPRAT HTML returned HTTP 403 in an earlier pass. The sentences are the indexed text of those URLs. How to tell the family from a snake is on the legless-vs-snake object. Patternless Delma, Delma inornata, was searched and was not returned within 50 km. It is not a local animal in this file.
habitat: Museums Victoria says grassy basalt plains, often under logs, rocks and leaf litter, and isolated populations in south-eastern mainland Australia (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8389). SPRAT's indexed text calls it a grassland specialist, found only in native grassland and nearby grassy woodland and exotic pasture, and says the primary habitat is covered by four nationally listed communities, including Natural Temperate Grassland of the Victorian Volcanic Plain and Grassy Eucalypt Woodland of the Victorian Volcanic Plain (https://www.environment.gov.au/cgi-bin/sprat/public/publicspecies.pl?taxon_id=1649). The 2016 conservation advice names those two Victorian communities among the four (https://www.environment.gov.au/biodiversity/threatened/species/pubs/1649-conservation-advice-16122016.pdf). Corangamite Catchment Management Authority's Grassy Eucalypt Woodlands Stewardship Program says those woodlands provide habitat for Striped Legless Lizards, and that the target region runs east from Shelford to the western flank of the You Yangs, south to Inverleigh and north to Meredith (https://ccma.vic.gov.au/projects/grassy-eucalypt-stewardship-program/). That is a regional program sentence. It is not a record inside 10 km of the centre. The Friends of Inverleigh Nature Conservation Reserve describe grassy woodland at the reserve. They do not list this lizard (https://inverleigh.org.au/features/nature-conservation/).
diet: Museums Victoria lists the diet as carnivore, insects and invertebrates (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8389). No local record exists inside 10 km from which to name a prey animal.
activeSeason: The Directory marks the species noctidiurnal (https://biodiversity.org.au/afd/taxa/Delma_impar). No month facet exists inside 10 km because the count is zero. Nearest dated rows outside the circle include 23 September 2011 and 4 November 2004 at Boonderoo Nature Conservation Reserve, and October 2004 and February and November 2007 near Cressy-Shelford Road. Those dates are not an Inverleigh activity calendar.
breeding: The Directory marks the species oviparous (https://biodiversity.org.au/afd/taxa/Delma_impar). Museums Victoria says animals can live more than 10 years and start mating after 3–4 years (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8389). Clutch size is not on the Directory page that was fetched or on the Museums Victoria extract. It is not filled from another site. No local nest exists in the 10 km search.
hangouts: None inside 5 km or 10 km. The nearest named places are outside the circle and are not Inverleigh. Victorian Biodiversity Atlas, 23 September 2011, one animal, Donna McMaster, captured and released, 'Boonderoo Nature Conservation Reserve Teesdale', -37.9674, 144.04631, about 14.75 km, uncertainty 10 m (https://biocache-ws.ala.org.au/ws/occurrence/b0d7fd92-e8c1-4774-962f-8be7fc9b7bcc). Victorian Biodiversity Atlas, 4 November 2004, one animal, Cath Grant, 'Boonderoo Nature Conservation Reserve', -37.96696, 144.04668, about 14.8 km, uncertainty 100 m (https://biocache-ws.ala.org.au/ws/occurrence/97de2fac-b6c7-468d-b3e8-6b3c49b4f86b). Museums Victoria OZCAM, locality 'Winchelsea', coordinate -38.23, 144.0 to two decimal degrees, about 15.1 km, no year and no uncertainty (https://biocache-ws.ala.org.au/ws/occurrence/2fd1baa6-a98b-4a89-ad5a-a6d092e5eeb2). That coordinate is too coarse to be a site. Further rows cluster on Cressy-Shelford Road, about 17.6 km, in 2004 and 2007 VBA and Museums Victoria samples. Geelong Field Naturalists Club, 10 September 2017, locality Paraparap, about 20.89 km, individual count 5, has a remark about calling frogs at Larcombe's Road nature reserve. The remark does not describe a lizard, so it is not used as behaviour for this species (https://biocache-ws.ala.org.au/ws/occurrence/bc4a6640-4c8a-432d-8b13-927f9eb94ccc). The animal is protected, and it is also listed, so the practical point is to leave grassland cover and not to treat a striped legless animal as a snake to be killed. identification: The lizards with accepted records inside 10 km are the Jacky lizard, the eastern three-lined skink, the garden skink, the eastern blue-tongue, the blotched blue-tongue, and, only in the outer ring, White's skink. The eastern snake-necked turtle is a turtle. The striped legless lizard was not returned inside 10 km. A small brown skink in a garden is not automatically a garden skink: one Inverleigh photo and one Bannockburn photo are still only family Scincidae.
habitat: The Australian Museum's blue-tongue account is the clearest local-yard description that was fetched in full: open country with tussocky grasses or leaf litter, and shelter under rocks and logs (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/reptiles/eastern-blue-tongue-lizard/). DEECA's Common Blue-tongued Lizard sheet says a lizard-friendly garden can leave logs and rocks on the ground for shelter (https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0019/84106/Common-Blue-tongued-Lizard.pdf). Museums Victoria says garden skinks use leaf litter and rock piles and suburban gardens (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/12372), and Jacky lizards bask on logs, fallen branches and rocks (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8368). The Inverleigh reserve's wallaby-grass ground layer is the vegetation of that reserve, not a planting recipe (https://inverleigh.org.au/features/nature-conservation/). This file does not invent a plant list, a pond or a basking paver specification.
diet: Blue-tongues eat snails and slugs as well as insects and some plants, which is why snail bait reaches them (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/reptiles/eastern-blue-tongue-lizard/; https://wildlifevictoria.org.au/learn/native-species-post/blue-tongued-lizard/). Garden skinks and the three-lined skink are invertebrate feeders on the Museums Victoria pages. Jacky lizards take small arthropods. Leaving those prey animals is the diet side of a garden. The DEECA sheet says never to feed blue-tongues (https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0019/84106/Common-Blue-tongued-Lizard.pdf).
activeSeason: The dated lizards in this batch are diurnal on the pages that say so. Blue-tongues are inactive in cold weather and may bask on sunny days. Small-skink rows include July. Record months are not a survey. See each species object.
breeding: Jacky lizards are egg-laying on the Directory, with no clutch size retrieved. Three-lined skinks lay up to five eggs, sometimes with other females. Garden skinks lay up to four eggs in communal nests. Both blue-tongues and White's skink give birth to live young. Litter numbers disagree between sources and are not repeated here. See each species.
hangouts: Named places that the records actually use are Inverleigh Nature Conservation Reserve or Inverleigh NCR, Inverleigh Conservation Reserve, Old Teesdale Track, Old Shelford Track, Inverleigh Common, the town place guesses Inverleigh VIC 3321 and Teesdale VIC 3328, Bannockburn and Bannockburn Bush, Harvey Road paddocks, Mason's Road with 900 m uncertainty, Spring Creek Road for one blue-tongue roadkill, and '7 km S of Inverleigh' for White's skink. Obscured iNaturalist coordinates are not hangouts. Tile grids at the repeated Bannockburn coordinate -38.052582, 144.134824 are survey shelters. No new spot is added.
threats: Snail and slug pellets: the Australian Museum says blue-tongues are poisoned by eating poisoned snails and slugs, including bait used next door (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/reptiles/eastern-blue-tongue-lizard/). Wildlife Victoria says snail bait is extremely dangerous and to call (03) 8400 7300 if it may have been eaten (https://wildlifevictoria.org.au/learn/native-species-post/blue-tongued-lizard/). The DEECA sheet says reduce or eliminate snail bait for the same reason (https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0019/84106/Common-Blue-tongued-Lizard.pdf). Better Health Channel says do not place baits where children, pets or native animals can reach them, and that a pesticide can harm an animal that eats a poisoned insect. The Victorian Poisons Information Centre is 13 11 26 (https://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/pest-control-in-the-home). No local snail-bait death was found in the rows. Mowers: the museum says blue-tongues hide in long grass rather than running (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/reptiles/eastern-blue-tongue-lizard/). Roads: the same page, the DEECA sheet, and the 25 May 2017 Spring Creek Road roadkill (https://biocache-ws.ala.org.au/ws/occurrence/9b700ea7-d2dd-42c7-bee6-9db904035adb). Cats: the DEECA species sheet says keep a cat indoors at night, and DEECA's protecting-wildlife page says keep your cat indoors (https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0019/84106/Common-Blue-tongued-Lizard.pdf; https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/protecting-wildlife/protecting-wildlife). Dogs and cats: Wildlife Victoria says attacks can be fatal (https://wildlifevictoria.org.au/learn/native-species-post/blue-tongued-lizard/). The museum also names suburban dogs and cats as predators of young blue-tongues. Those pet sentences are blue-tongue evidence. They were not matched to a Jacky, a garden skink or a three-lined skink row. Logs and rocks left on the ground are the shelter the DEECA sheet and the museum describe. The Conservation Regulator says routine mowing that unintentionally disturbs wildlife does not need an Authority to Control Wildlife, and that relocating wildlife does (https://www.vic.gov.au/authority-control-wildlife-application-guide). Wildlife Victoria still describes sliding a blue-tongue onto a towel to move it away from a dog. Both sentences are reported. Injured wildlife: Wildlife Victoria (03) 8400 7300, DEECA 136 186 (https://www.zoo.org.au/emergency-wildlife-help/).
conservation: The six lizard species with rows inside 10 km are not on the FFG Threatened List of July 2026 and are not on the EPBC extract of 28 August 2026 as those species. The northern blue-tongue subspecies is EPBC Critically Endangered and is not marked for Victoria. The striped legless lizard is EPBC Vulnerable and FFG Endangered and was not recorded inside 10 km. Every native reptile is still protected under the Wildlife Act 1975 (https://www.vic.gov.au/authority-control-wildlife-application-guide). A Golden Plains Shire page about lizards was not found.
notWellDocumented: No local snail-bait death, cat attack or mower injury was found. The threats are the museum, Wildlife Victoria and DEECA accounts, plus one roadkill.
The DEECA species sheet says cats indoors at night. The protecting-wildlife page says keep the cat indoors. Both are cited and not merged into a single rule.

records.whatThisObjectIs: Not a species. How to tell a legless lizard from a snake, and the honest local result that no legless lizard was returned inside 10 km.

identification: Legless lizards in the family Pygopodidae are lizards, related to geckos, not snakes. The Australian Faunal Directory diagnosis for the family says the forelimbs are absent, the hind limbs are a pair of scaly flaps beside the cloaca, the eyes have no movable lids and are covered by a spectacle, an external ear opening is usually present, and the tail, unless it is regrowing, is usually at least as long as the snout-vent length (https://biodiversity.org.au/afd/taxa/Pygopodidae). SPRAT's account of the striped legless lizard says it can be distinguished from a snake by external ear openings, a fleshy undivided tongue, and a tail longer than the body (https://www.environment.gov.au/cgi-bin/sprat/public/publicspecies.pl?taxon_id=1649). Museums Victoria says the tongue is not forked and the ears are visible (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8389). A Land for Wildlife newsletter says legless lizards are not snakes, that snakes lack eyelids and external ears while most lizards have them, and that many legless lizards have tiny flaps. It also says the tongue difference is not obvious to a startled observer, and that the photos of a striped legless lizard show the ear opening and the flaps. Except for the Hooded Scaly-foot, which that page limits to northern Victorian grasslands, legless lizards do not have a black head. A slaty-grey head is possible (https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0031/692554/LFW_Newsletter_2022.pdf). The eyelid sentence needs the Directory's caveat: pygopodids have a spectacle and no movable lids, so 'snakes have no eyelids and lizards do' does not separate this family from a snake. Use the ear, the flap, the tongue and the long tail, and do not pick the animal up to check. The Hooded Scaly-foot is not a local record: genus Pygopus returned 0 rows within 50 km. Patternless Delma also returned 0 within 50 km.
habitat: See the striped-legless-lizard object. No legless-lizard habitat was recorded inside 10 km. The Corangamite CMA stewardship region names the striped legless lizard and includes Inverleigh as its southern edge. That is not a sighting (https://ccma.vic.gov.au/projects/grassy-eucalypt-stewardship-program/).
diet: Not a separate diet. Museums Victoria lists insects for the striped legless lizard. Local snakes are a different batch.
activeSeason: The Directory marks Delma impar noctidiurnal. There is no local month count.
breeding: The Directory marks Delma impar oviparous. Clutch size was not retrieved. Snakes in the previous batch include live-bearing elapids. Breeding method is not a safe field test.
hangouts: No legless-lizard hangout inside 10 km. The nearest named striped legless lizard places are Boonderoo Nature Conservation Reserve at Teesdale, about 14.8 km, and coarser points further out. They are listed on the striped-legless-lizard object and are not Inverleigh.
threats: The harm in a mistaken identity is treating a legless lizard as a snake to be killed, or picking up a small snake to look for an ear. Both are avoided by leaving the animal alone. If someone is bitten and the animal might be a snake, use snake-bite first aid and call triple zero (000). The Better Health Channel bites-and-stings page is the Victorian first-aid page already used for the local snakes (https://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/bites-and-stings-first-aid). This object does not repeat the bandage steps. Killing or taking a native reptile without a permit is an offence under the Wildlife Act 1975 (https://www.vic.gov.au/authority-control-wildlife-application-guide).
conservation: The only pygopodid in the wider ALA search was Delma impar, which is EPBC Vulnerable and FFG Endangered. It was not inside 10 km. Details are on the striped-legless-lizard object. Other listed legless lizards on the EPBC extract, including Aprasia parapulchella and Aprasia aurita, had no genus records within 50 km.
notWellDocumented: No legless lizard of any genus was returned inside 10 km. Absence in the databases is not a promise that one will never be seen.
The Land for Wildlife eyelid sentence is not a reliable test for pygopodids, which have a spectacle.
Ear, flap and tongue are the published differences, and the newsletter says they are not obvious when the person is startled.
The Hooded Scaly-foot exception is not a local record.
SPRAT HTML was 403. The ear, tongue and tail sentences are indexed text of that profile.
Do not handle the animal to confirm the characters.
